items.prompt: A design system has existed and been the source of truth for three years. A squad ships a one-off button variant outside the spec under deadline pressure. Is this visual drift or design debt?
choices: Visual drift — drift is just any inconsistency anywhere in a UI, so an existing three-year-old system doesn't change the classification
Design debt — it's a deliberate one-off departure from an already-existing system, not teams independently reinventing something because no shared system exists yet
Neither — a single button variant stays too small to count as either one until it spreads to multiple screens and squads over time
It's design debt only if the button variant ships with an actual functional bug attached to it
items.explanation: Visual drift is what happens before a shared system exists (independent reinvention). Design debt is what accumulates inside a system that already exists, through deliberate exceptions that don't get reconciled — this is the debt case.
items.reference:
Visual driftNo shared system yet; independent reinvention
Design debtSystem exists; deliberate exceptions accumulate inside it

Why: the presence of an existing source of truth is what distinguishes the two.

items.prompt: Which scenario best matches the definition of design debt rather than visual drift?
choices: Two squads, before any shared design system exists, each build their own slightly different primary button
A mature design system's official spec is bypassed by a deadline-driven exception that never gets reconciled back into it
A brand-new startup's only designer picks a blue without writing it down anywhere
A font renders slightly differently across two browsers due to rendering engine differences
items.explanation: Design debt specifically requires an existing system being bypassed and the bypass never getting resolved — the other options describe pre-system drift or unrelated rendering quirks.
items.reference:
Visual driftNo shared system yet; independent reinvention
Design debtSystem exists; deliberate exceptions accumulate inside it

Why: the presence of an existing source of truth is what distinguishes the two.

items.prompt: A squad copies a shared component into their own codebase, intending to reconcile it with the original later, to move faster under deadline pressure. Which of the four accumulation modes is this?
choices: Governance decay
Orphaned component
Silent forking
One-off exception that never gets reconciled
items.explanation: Silent forking is specifically copying a component to move independently, with the two copies then drifting apart because the promised later reconciliation doesn't happen.
items.reference:
1. One-off exceptions never reconciled
2. Orphaned components
3. Governance decay
4. Silent forking

Why: each mode has a distinct mechanism — knowing which one you're looking at points to a different fix.

items.prompt: A component still sits in the shared library, but the feature it was built for was redesigned two years ago and nothing currently imports it. Which accumulation mode is this?
choices: Orphaned component
Silent forking
Visual drift
One-off exception that never gets reconciled
items.explanation: An orphaned component is one that remains in the library or codebase with no current real usage — it survives as a false option the next search will surface.
items.reference:
1. One-off exceptions never reconciled
2. Orphaned components
3. Governance decay
4. Silent forking

Why: each mode has a distinct mechanism — knowing which one you're looking at points to a different fix.

items.prompt: The design-system review process (a required sign-off before merging a new component) quietly stops being enforced after a reorg, with nobody deciding this on purpose. Which mode is this?
choices: Silent forking
Governance decay
Orphaned component
Visual drift
items.explanation: Governance decay is the process that used to catch exceptions quietly stopping — often through organizational change rather than a deliberate decision to remove it.
items.reference:
1. One-off exceptions never reconciled
2. Orphaned components
3. Governance decay
4. Silent forking

Why: each mode has a distinct mechanism — knowing which one you're looking at points to a different fix.

items.prompt: Why does a single unreconciled exception tend to spread rather than stay isolated?
choices: It doesn't spread on its own — each exception stays isolated to the one screen it was originally built for, with no further copying
Because the next engineer under deadline pressure searches the codebase, finds the exception already in use, and assumes it's sanctioned
Because design tools automatically propagate any newly built component out to every other screen in the product
Because design systems require every component to already be in use on at least two screens before it counts
items.explanation: An unreconciled exception looks, from the outside, indistinguishable from a sanctioned component — so the next person under pressure copies it rather than building something new, spreading it further.
items.reference:
Deadline pressure → one-off exception ships → not reviewed/fixed → becomes invisible precedent → copied at the next deadline → repeats.

Why: an unreviewed exception is indistinguishable from a sanctioned component to whoever finds it next.

items.prompt: What breaks a single exception's small, individually-reasonable justification into a larger systemic problem?
choices: The exception itself slowly getting more visually complex and harder to maintain over time, independent of review
It failing to get reviewed and either fixed or formally adopted, so it becomes invisible precedent for the next deadline
The design system's official spec being accidentally deleted from the shared component library
Users noticing the visual inconsistency on their own and filing complaints about it to support
items.explanation: The individual exception doesn't have to change at all — what matters is whether it gets resolved (fixed or adopted) or left to sit as something the next person can copy.
items.reference:
Deadline pressure → one-off exception ships → not reviewed/fixed → becomes invisible precedent → copied at the next deadline → repeats.

Why: an unreviewed exception is indistinguishable from a sanctioned component to whoever finds it next.

items.prompt: For a design system with one designer and one engineer total, what does 'governance' typically mean in practice?
choices: A formal, documented, standing review process with a rotating owner role
The person who built it still remembers every decision that was made
An automated CI gate that blocks any undocumented component
A quarterly all-hands presentation about the design system
items.explanation: At very small scale, informal memory can substitute for a formal process — the two people who built the system simply remember the reasoning behind every decision. This stops scaling almost immediately as headcount and screen count grow.
items.reference:
Small scale: memory substitutes for process. At scale: memory doesn't cover enough people or decisions, so a standing process is required.

Why: what 'governance' needs to mean changes as the system and org grow, even if nobody redefines the word.

items.prompt: What is the key ingredient a governance process needs once a design system has real scale (many squads, many screens), that informal memory can't provide?
choices: A bigger Figma file that documents more screens, without any change to who owns reviewing new exceptions as they appear
A standing process: someone owns reviewing exceptions, a documented threshold for adopting vs. deleting them, and a regular audit for orphaned components
A stricter visual style with fewer allowed colors and typefaces, enforced the same informal way the smaller system already was
Mandatory design training for every new engineer joining a squad, in place of an ongoing review and audit process
items.explanation: Scale requires the review responsibility, the decision criteria, and the audit cadence to all be explicit and standing — not dependent on any one person's memory of past decisions.
items.reference:
Small scale: memory substitutes for process. At scale: memory doesn't cover enough people or decisions, so a standing process is required.

Why: what 'governance' needs to mean changes as the system and org grow, even if nobody redefines the word.

items.prompt: Northwind's design system, four years in, had 37 button variants against a spec that listed 3. What does L1 conclude this means about the system?
choices: The system was poorly designed from the start, and better upfront planning would have kept the variant count near zero for good
Every system under real deadline pressure for years accumulates some debt — the differentiator is whether anything actively pays it down, not whether debt appeared at all
The team should have picked a different design tool that enforces stricter component reuse
The system should be rebuilt entirely from scratch every two years specifically to avoid ever accumulating this kind of variant sprawl
items.explanation: Debt accumulation is treated as close to inevitable under sustained real-world pressure. What separates a coherent system from a patchwork one is active, scheduled debt paydown, not the absence of any debt ever appearing.
items.reference:
Debt appearing ≠ system failure. Debt never being paid down = system decay.

Why: the useful question isn't 'did debt appear' but 'is anything actively resolving it.'

items.prompt: What is the actual differentiator between a design system that stays coherent for years and one that decays into an unexplained patchwork?
choices: Whether the original design team that built the system is still employed at the company today
Whether the system still has a modern-looking visual style after several years of real use
Whether debt is being actively identified and resolved on a schedule, rather than just whether debt ever appears
Whether the system uses design tokens at all, regardless of whether anyone audits them
items.explanation: Both a healthy and a decayed system will accumulate exceptions under deadline pressure — the difference is entirely in whether a process exists to find and resolve that debt on an ongoing basis.
items.reference:
Debt appearing ≠ system failure. Debt never being paid down = system decay.

Why: the useful question isn't 'did debt appear' but 'is anything actively resolving it.'

items.prompt: What specifically makes a component 'orphaned' rather than simply 'a variant that's still used but not in the spec'?
choices: It's simply older than a year, regardless of whether it's still referenced by any shipping screen
It's still in the library or codebase, but nothing (or almost nothing) currently shipping actually needs it
It has a name that nobody on the current team remembers or can explain anymore
It was originally built by someone who has since left the company entirely
items.explanation: Orphaned specifically means unused, not merely undocumented — an undocumented-but-actively-used component is the compact-card, one-off-exception shape, a different problem with a different fix (adopt or delete via the test) than an orphan (retire it).
items.reference:
Orphan = unused, still present. One-off exception = used, undocumented. Different problems, different fixes.

Why: confusing 'unused' with 'undocumented' leads to the wrong remediation.

items.prompt: A component is fully documented in the spec, has an owner, but the feature that used it was removed from the product last quarter, and no screen currently references it. Is this an orphaned component?
choices: No — because it's documented and has a named owner, and orphaned status is defined as requiring the component to be undocumented as well
Yes — orphaned status is about current usage, not documentation quality; a well-documented but unused component is still an orphan
No, only components that were never formally adopted in the first place can become orphans
Yes, but only once its original owner also leaves the company for good
items.explanation: Documentation and ownership don't prevent orphaning — they describe how well a component was governed when adopted, not whether it's still needed. Usage, not paperwork, determines orphan status.
items.reference:
Orphan = unused, still present. One-off exception = used, undocumented. Different problems, different fixes.

Why: confusing 'unused' with 'undocumented' leads to the wrong remediation.

items.prompt: An exception solves a real, recurring need and its difference from the existing component is intentional (not accidental drift), but formalizing it would cost far more than the confusion of leaving it informal costs. Per the adopt-vs-delete test, what's the outcome?
choices: Adopt it anyway, since passing the first two of the three questions is treated as enough even if the cost question answers no
Delete it — a 'no' on any one of the three questions routes to delete, there's no partial-credit adoption
Leave it undecided for now and revisit the decision once usage grows further
Escalate it to leadership for a one-off, case-by-case exception outside the test
items.explanation: The test requires all three questions to answer yes before adopting. A 'no' on the cost question alone is enough to route to delete, regardless of how the first two questions answered.
items.reference:
Real distinct need?No → delete
Intentional, not drift?No → delete
Cheaper to formalize than leave informal?No → delete

Why: all three must be yes to adopt; there's no 'leave as is' third outcome.

items.prompt: What is the third and final question in the adopt-vs-delete test, once an exception has already passed 'solves a real need' and 'the difference is intentional'?
choices: Does the design team simply prefer how the exception looks compared to the component it's diverging from in the spec
Would formalizing it (tokens, docs, ownership) cost less than the ongoing confusion of leaving it informal?
Has the exception been in active use for at least six consecutive months already
Did the exception originate from a senior designer rather than a junior one
items.explanation: The third question weighs the one-time cost of formalizing against the ongoing, compounding cost of leaving the exception undecided — that comparison, not tenure or popularity, decides the outcome.
items.reference:
Real distinct need?No → delete
Intentional, not drift?No → delete
Cheaper to formalize than leave informal?No → delete

Why: all three must be yes to adopt; there's no 'leave as is' third outcome.

items.prompt: Why does the adopt-vs-delete test have exactly two possible outcomes (adopt or delete) rather than three (adopt, delete, or leave as is)?
choices: Because leaving an exception undecided is what let it spread and get copied as invisible precedent in the first place — 'leave it' is what produced the problem, not a valid resolution to it
Because a three-outcome test, with adopt, delete, and leave-as-is as separate results, would be too complicated to run inside a normal design review cadence
Because deleting is always the cheaper of the two options, so it's treated as the safe default
Because design tools don't technically support marking a component with a 'pending' status
items.explanation: The compact-card story shows exactly why 'leave it' isn't neutral: an undecided exception keeps getting found and copied by the next deadline-pressured engineer, exactly like a sanctioned component would be.
items.reference:
Real distinct need?No → delete
Intentional, not drift?No → delete
Cheaper to formalize than leave informal?No → delete

Why: all three must be yes to adopt; there's no 'leave as is' third outcome.

items.prompt: An unreviewed exception is currently used on nine screens across three squads. What does that usage count actually tell you, per L2?
choices: That the component is well-designed on its own merits across all nine screens and should therefore definitely be formally adopted
That unreviewed components get copied just as readily as reviewed ones — usage alone isn't evidence the component is good, only that it's overdue for a decision
That the component should be immediately deleted outright, regardless of what need it serves
Nothing at all — usage counts are treated as fully irrelevant to any governance decision
items.explanation: High usage of an unreviewed exception is evidence of copying under deadline pressure (the silent-forking-adjacent pattern), not evidence of quality — the adopt-vs-delete test still has to be run on its merits.
items.reference:
9 screens using it ≠ 9 independent endorsements of quality. It's evidence the decision is overdue, not evidence of the right decision.

Why: usage spreads identically whether a component is reviewed or not.

items.prompt: Why is 'it's already used on many screens, so let's just keep it' a risky governance instinct?
choices: Because screens that reference a larger number of distinct shared components are always measurably slower for users to load
Because it treats spread caused by unreviewed copying as if it were spread caused by deliberate, evaluated adoption — the two look identical from usage counts alone
Because a healthy design system should never have more than a small handful of components
Because it's technically infeasible for engineering to ever remove a widely-used component
items.explanation: Usage count doesn't distinguish 'many teams evaluated this and chose it' from 'many teams found it unreviewed and assumed it was safe' — only running the actual test does.
items.reference:
9 screens using it ≠ 9 independent endorsements of quality. It's evidence the decision is overdue, not evidence of the right decision.

Why: usage spreads identically whether a component is reviewed or not.

items.prompt: A governance model where a dedicated design-system team reviews and decides every exception across the whole org has what characteristic weakness?
choices: It tends to produce inconsistent, contradictory decisions across different squads and product areas
It becomes a throughput bottleneck as the org grows, and is often the first team cut under budget or reorg pressure
It's structurally unable to run the adopt-vs-delete test on any exception it's handed
It requires no dedicated headcount at all, unlike the federated or automated-gate models
items.explanation: A centralized team gives consistent decisions but has fixed capacity — as squads and screens multiply, review throughput doesn't scale with them, and the team's small size makes it an easy target in a reorg.
items.reference:
CentralizedConsistent, but bottlenecks and is cut-risk
FederatedScales, but owners drift without a shared forum
Automated gateCatches early, but no judgment, needs tooling

Why: no single model eliminates the need for the test — each changes who runs it and when.

items.prompt: In a federated stewardship model with no shared cross-area forum, what failure mode tends to recur?
choices: Nothing in particular changes — a federated model is described as carrying no meaningful governance weaknesses of its own
Three product areas quietly adopt three slightly different solutions to the same underlying need — drift reappears, just one layer up from individual screens
The design system stops having any governance process running anywhere in the org
Only the centralized team's original founding members retain the authority to decide
items.explanation: Federated stewardship scales review capacity with the org, but without a way for owners to compare notes, independent-but-similar decisions across areas reproduce drift at the component level instead of the screen level.
items.reference:
CentralizedConsistent, but bottlenecks and is cut-risk
FederatedScales, but owners drift without a shared forum
Automated gateCatches early, but no judgment, needs tooling

Why: no single model eliminates the need for the test — each changes who runs it and when.

items.prompt: An automated CI gate that blocks any new component with no linked spec entry has what limitation, per L2?
choices: It requires no tooling investment at all, in contrast to both the centralized model and the federated stewardship model
It catches exceptions at creation time, which is valuable, but it enforces documentation, not judgment — it can't itself decide whether an exception should be adopted or deleted
It only works for organizations that have exactly one single product area to govern
It's described as strictly worse for a design system than running no gate at all
items.explanation: An automated gate is good at catching the moment an undocumented component would merge, but the actual adopt-vs-delete judgment still requires a human evaluating the three-question test — the gate enforces process, not the decision itself.
items.reference:
CentralizedConsistent, but bottlenecks and is cut-risk
FederatedScales, but owners drift without a shared forum
Automated gateCatches early, but no judgment, needs tooling

Why: no single model eliminates the need for the test — each changes who runs it and when.

items.prompt: Why doesn't running the adopt-vs-delete test on new exceptions automatically catch orphaned components?
choices: Because orphaned components are described as a theoretical category that doesn't actually technically exist in most real codebases
Because that test runs on new exceptions being created, while an orphan is an old, once-correctly-adopted component that became unused later — a different event the test was never watching for
Because the test only applies to components created in the specific calendar quarter immediately following a reorg announcement
Because orphaned components are automatically deleted by the build tooling the moment their last reference disappears
items.explanation: The adopt-vs-delete test is triggered by a new exception appearing. An orphan is created by a feature being removed or redesigned around an already-adopted component — a separate event that needs its own, scheduled check.
items.reference:
New-exception review and orphan detection are two different, independent checks — one triggered by creation, one needing a recurring usage audit.

Why: a component can be adopted correctly and still become an orphan years later.

items.prompt: What kind of check is needed, independent of exception review, to catch components that have become orphaned?
choices: A one-time check that's performed only once, at the moment the design system first launches, with nothing scheduled afterward
A recurring, scheduled audit of every component currently in the library against what's actually referenced by shipping code, with someone responsible for retiring the unused ones
A survey that simply asks designers whether they personally recall using a component recently
Relying on engineers to notice and voluntarily report orphans, with no scheduled check at all
items.explanation: Because orphaning happens silently (a feature gets redesigned, nothing forces removal of what it used to depend on), catching it requires an ongoing, scheduled usage audit, not a one-time or informal check.
items.reference:
New-exception review and orphan detection are two different, independent checks — one triggered by creation, one needing a recurring usage audit.

Why: a component can be adopted correctly and still become an orphan years later.

items.prompt: A design system's original team is disbanded in a reorg and nobody is assigned to run the adopt-vs-delete test afterward. Deadline pressure on other squads doesn't change. What happens to the rate at which new exceptions are built during this gap?
choices: The rate of new exceptions being built drops all the way to zero, since there's nobody left in place reviewing or approving them
New exceptions keep appearing at roughly the same rate as before — building a one-off under deadline pressure was always faster than finding and reusing the sanctioned component, review or no review
New exceptions only start appearing roughly once a year, timed deliberately to the org's scheduled annual planning cycle
Squads stop building anything new whatsoever until formal governance has been fully restored across every product area
items.explanation: Removing the review step doesn't remove the underlying pressure that produces exceptions — engineers and designers still face the same deadlines. What stops is the resolution step, not the creation rate.
items.reference:
Governance gap: exception creation rate stays the same; only the resolve-to-adopt-or-delete step disappears. Nothing crashes visibly during the gap — that's what makes it dangerous.

Why: an invisible failure mode is still a failure mode — the absence of a review step doesn't announce itself.

items.prompt: During a governance gap, why doesn't the design system visibly break, even though debt is actively accumulating?
choices: Because no new exceptions are actually being created by any squad for the entire duration of the governance gap itself

Because each individual exception still ships working code for its own screen — nothing crashes; the cost is invisible accumulation that only surfaces later, e.g. when an audit or incident eventually exposes it
Because automated tests are described as independently catching and blocking every new exception the moment it's introduced
Because the design system's component library is described as becoming fully read-only once its team gets disbanded
items.explanation: Each exception, taken alone, is a working piece of shipped UI — nothing about it fails on its own. The cost is systemic and cumulative, which is exactly why it can go unnoticed for a long time.
items.reference:
Governance gap: exception creation rate stays the same; only the resolve-to-adopt-or-delete step disappears. Nothing crashes visibly during the gap — that's what makes it dangerous.

Why: an invisible failure mode is still a failure mode — the absence of a review step doesn't announce itself.

items.prompt: A component was adopted correctly five years ago, with a full spec and a named owner. Can it still become an orphan?
choices: No — a component that was correctly adopted with a full spec and a named owner is described as never becoming an orphan later on
Yes — if the feature it served gets redesigned or removed and nothing ever forces its removal from the library, it becomes unused regardless of how well it was originally governed
No, only components that were adopted without ever being assigned an owner can become orphans
Yes, but only in the specific case where the component's original owner leaves the company
items.explanation: Correct adoption governs the moment a component is created, not what happens to it years later — orphaning is driven by later feature changes, which a one-time adoption process can't anticipate.
items.reference:
New-exception review and orphan detection are two different, independent checks — one triggered by creation, one needing a recurring usage audit.

Why: a component can be adopted correctly and still become an orphan years later.

items.prompt: In Northwind's year-1 to year-3 story, what specifically caused the eleven-day median resolution time to grow into a backlog, even though the review process itself didn't change?
choices: The three-person review team simply started reviewing each incoming exception less carefully as their own workload grew over time
The org grew from 40 to 340 screens across eleven squads while the review team stayed at three people — throughput mismatch, not a change in process quality
The design system's tooling broke down and silently stopped tracking exceptions being created
Leadership made an explicit, stated decision to deprioritize design-system governance entirely
items.explanation: The process itself was unchanged; what changed was the ratio of exception volume (growing with squads and screens) to fixed review capacity (three people) — a scale mismatch, not a quality regression.
items.reference:
Year 1: 40 screens, 3 reviewers, 11-day median. Year 3: 340 screens, still 3 reviewers, growing backlog. Same process, different throughput demand.

Why: a fixed-capacity centralized model doesn't scale with org growth on its own.

items.prompt: After Northwind's year-3 reorg redistributed the design-system team, why did the adopt-vs-delete process stop running even though no one explicitly decided to end it?
choices: Leadership issued a formal, explicit memo announcing that the design system's governance process was being discontinued company-wide
The org chart no longer had a role whose job it was to run the test — it fell through the gap between eleven newly autonomous squads, none formally designated as stewards
The design system's token definitions were accidentally deleted as part of the reorg itself
Engineers collectively refused to keep complying with the review process going forward
items.explanation: The lapse was structural, not a decision — three specific people's job function disappeared from the new org chart, and nothing else was put in its place, so review stopped by omission rather than by choice.
items.reference:
Year 1: 40 screens, 3 reviewers, 11-day median. Year 3: 340 screens, still 3 reviewers, growing backlog. Same process, different throughput demand.

Why: a fixed-capacity centralized model doesn't scale with org growth on its own.

items.prompt: The urgent-banner component caused a customer-visible incident when reused for a flash sale. What was the root cause, per the postmortem described in L3?
choices: The engineer who reused the urgent-banner component simply made a careless mistake that more thorough training would have prevented

The component had no documented spec explaining its narrow original purpose (a one-time, non-dismissible outage notice), because the governance step that would have caught this had lapsed eighteen months earlier
The design system's color tokens had been misconfigured somewhere upstream, which is what caused the banner to misbehave
The flash-sale campaign that reused the banner component was shipped without going through design review at all
items.explanation: The postmortem's finding was structural: nothing distinguished a narrow-purpose component from a general-reuse one because the documentation and review step that should have caught the mismatch had quietly stopped running.
items.reference:
Urgent-banner: built non-dismissible for a genuine one-time outage. Reused, undocumented, for a recurring flash sale. Non-dismissible behavior became a user-facing bug.

Why: the component's original assumptions weren't wrong for its original purpose — they were wrong for the purpose it got reused for, invisibly.

items.prompt: Why was the urgent-banner component non-dismissible in a way that caused real user harm when reused for a promotion, when that same behavior was appropriate for its original purpose?
choices: Non-dismissible behavior on any banner component is described as always being a bug outright, regardless of the surrounding context it ships in

It was built correctly for a rare, temporary, site-wide outage notice, where non-dismissibility is appropriate — but that assumption doesn't transfer to a recurring promotional banner, and nothing documented the assumption for the next team to catch
The original engineer who built the component is described as having always intended for it to eventually be reused for recurring promotions
The component's underlying code contained an unrelated bug that had nothing to do with its original, narrow design intent
items.explanation: The component wasn't defective — it correctly implemented its original, narrow purpose. The harm came from reusing it outside that purpose with no documentation to flag the mismatched assumption.
items.reference:
Urgent-banner: built non-dismissible for a genuine one-time outage. Reused, undocumented, for a recurring flash sale. Non-dismissible behavior became a user-facing bug.

Why: the component's original assumptions weren't wrong for its original purpose — they were wrong for the purpose it got reused for, invisibly.

items.prompt: Northwind's remediation ran a full inventory before triage, rather than triaging issues in the order they were discovered. Why?
choices: Inventory-first is simply described as the standard step required by most mainstream project-management methodologies used across the industry
Triaging in discovery order without a full inventory would just repeat the informal, whoever-notices-first process that already failed — a full picture is needed before prioritizing what to fix
It's actually faster overall to inventory everything first, independent of any accuracy benefit it brings
Because the CI gate itself required a fully complete component list to exist before it could be turned on
items.explanation: Triage without a full inventory reproduces exactly the ad hoc, notice-it-when-you-see-it pattern that let the debt accumulate invisibly in the first place — the inventory is what lets prioritization be deliberate.
items.reference:
1. Full inventory (61 orphans, 34 undocumented-but-used, 1 misused-but-documented). 2. Triage by usage + user-facing risk. 3. Restore a governance model sized to actual org shape.

Why: each step depends on the one before it — skipping the inventory undermines the triage that follows.

items.prompt: During triage, Northwind prioritized high-usage, undocumented components over the 61 zero-usage orphans. What was the reasoning?
choices: Orphans are described as always being inherently easier to fix than undocumented-but-used components, so they were deferred purely out of convenience

A high-usage, undocumented component (the urgent-banner-shaped risk — wrong assumptions baked into something widely reused) posed more active risk than a zero-usage orphan sitting harmlessly unreferenced
The 61 orphans were deleted first simply because deleting is treated as always the correct first move
Usage count was treated as irrelevant to prioritization; components were instead triaged alphabetically
items.explanation: A component nobody uses can't cause a live incident. A widely-reused, undocumented component with unreviewed assumptions can — and did, which is why it was weighted higher in triage order even though there were far more orphans by count.
items.reference:
1. Full inventory (61 orphans, 34 undocumented-but-used, 1 misused-but-documented). 2. Triage by usage + user-facing risk. 3. Restore a governance model sized to actual org shape.

Why: each step depends on the one before it — skipping the inventory undermines the triage that follows.

items.prompt: After the incident, Northwind rejected simply restoring a single centralized team of three. Why?
choices: Because centralized teams are described as never being an appropriate governance model for any design system at any scale whatsoever
Because that model had already demonstrably failed to scale once (the year-3 throughput mismatch) and the org kept growing, so the same failure would very likely recur
Because leadership refused outright to fund any headcount for governance going forward at all
Because the CI tooling alone made a human review team entirely unnecessary going forward
items.explanation: The choice was informed directly by the year-3 history: a fixed-capacity centralized team had already broken down once under growth, so restoring the identical model without addressing the scale mismatch would predictably repeat the failure.
items.reference:
Chosen model: one steward per product area (federated) + automated spec-linked CI gate + monthly cross-area forum, sized to eleven squads rather than the original three-person team.

Why: the right governance model depends on the org's actual shape, not the shape it had at launch.

items.prompt: What three elements made up the governance model Northwind restored after the incident?
choices: A single new centralized team of three, a bigger review budget, and a rebranded version of the exact same original design system
A designated steward per product area, an automated CI gate requiring a linked spec entry, and a shared monthly forum for stewards to reconcile drift between areas
Mandatory design certification required for every engineer, plus a stricter visual style guide
Outsourcing all design-system maintenance work going forward to an external agency
items.explanation: The restored model combined federated stewardship (scales with org size) with an automated gate (catches issues at creation time) and a shared forum (prevents the federated model's own drift-between-areas weakness) — addressing each model's known weakness from L2's table.
items.reference:
Chosen model: one steward per product area (federated) + automated spec-linked CI gate + monthly cross-area forum, sized to eleven squads rather than the original three-person team.

Why: the right governance model depends on the org's actual shape, not the shape it had at launch.

items.prompt: Northwind's automated CI gate allows a squad to merge an undocumented component under deadline pressure via an explicit, time-boxed exception flag rather than an outright block. Why is that better than a hard block with no exception path?
choices: A hard block with no exception path is described as being technically impossible to implement in most modern CI pipeline systems

A hard block would likely push squads toward silent forking (copying components to route around the gate), recreating an undocumented exception invisibly rather than a visible, dated one the gate and future audits can still track
Exception flags are described as removing the need for any future review of the flagged component once they're applied
It has no real governance benefit at all; the exception path exists purely as a developer convenience with no tracking value
items.explanation: An absolute block under real deadline pressure just relocates the same undocumented-exception problem outside the gate's visibility. A visible, dated exception flag keeps the record the monthly forum needs to eventually run the adopt-vs-delete test on it.
items.reference:
Hard block → risk of silent forking around the gate. Time-boxed exception flag → visible, dated record the steward forum can act on later.

Why: the goal is visibility of exceptions, not zero exceptions ever shipping under pressure.

items.prompt: What does a time-boxed exception flag on an undocumented component actually accomplish that an informal 'we'll deal with it later' verbal agreement wouldn't?
choices: Nothing meaningfully different — both the flag and the verbal agreement are described as relying entirely on someone simply remembering to follow up later

It creates a visible, dated record that surfaces the component on a list due for the adopt-vs-delete test by a specific date, instead of relying on memory the way the original urgent-banner exception did
It automatically deletes the component once its deadline passes, with no human decision required
It grants the component permanent adopted status outright, with no further review ever required
items.explanation: The value is turning an informal intention into a trackable, dated artifact a governance process can act on — exactly the record that was missing for the urgent-banner component and let it sit undocumented for years.
items.reference:
Hard block → risk of silent forking around the gate. Time-boxed exception flag → visible, dated record the steward forum can act on later.

Why: the goal is visibility of exceptions, not zero exceptions ever shipping under pressure.

items.prompt: Northwind's remediation took roughly nine person-weeks. How does L3 frame this cost relative to the incident it followed?
choices: Nine person-weeks was judged roughly comparable to the six-hour incident's own support and postmortem cost, making the remediation a break-even trade rather than a clear saving
It was a fraction of the cost of the six-hour incident's support load, postmortem, and reputational damage — the remediation was cheaper than the failure it was responding to
The remediation's cost was never actually compared against the incident's cost anywhere in the account given
The remediation was funded without regard to cost, since design-system work is treated as having no measurable ROI
items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames the nine-week remediation as non-trivial but smaller than what the visible incident cost — a concrete argument for paying debt down proactively rather than only after a forcing incident.
items.reference:
Remediation: ~9 person-weeks. Incident: 6 hours of customer-visible harm, support spike, postmortem, reputational cost. Year-5 resolution rate rebounded to ~82%, near the original year-1 rate.

Why: proactive debt paydown is cheaper than the incident that eventually forces it.

items.prompt: Why did Northwind's exception-resolution rate rebound to roughly its year-1 level (about 82% within 30 days) after the remediation, rather than staying degraded even with a new governance model in place?
choices: Because the new federated-plus-gate model is described as being inherently smarter in its judgment than the original three-person centralized team ever was

Because the new model was sized to eleven squads' actual exception volume instead of being capped at three people's fixed review capacity — matching capacity to demand, not a different quality of decision-making
Because the overall rate of new exceptions being created dropped sharply right after the incident itself
Because the company is described as having simply stopped growing headcount after year five
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the rebound wasn't about the new model being smarter — it was about right-sizing review capacity to the org's actual scale, the exact mismatch that caused the year-3 backlog in the first place.
items.reference:
Remediation: ~9 person-weeks. Incident: 6 hours of customer-visible harm, support spike, postmortem, reputational cost. Year-5 resolution rate rebounded to ~82%, near the original year-1 rate.

Why: proactive debt paydown is cheaper than the incident that eventually forces it.

items.prompt: L3 closes by asking what would change about Northwind's remediation if debt had stayed invisible for years with no single dramatic incident ever forcing leadership to fund an inventory. What is the most likely change, reasoning from the case as given?
choices: Nothing would need to change at all — the same nine-week remediation playbook would still get funded automatically on the exact same schedule

The case for funding step one (the inventory) would need to rest on slower, harder-to-point-to costs — onboarding drag, search friction, accumulated confusion — rather than a single incident report leadership can react to directly
The playbook itself would need to skip straight to triage, since a full inventory is described as only mattering once an incident has already occurred
Design debt that never causes a visible incident is described as not actually being a real cost worth addressing in the first place
items.explanation: The three-step playbook (inventory, triage, right-sized governance) doesn't depend on having an incident to justify it — but the funding argument does need to change, from 'here is what just happened' to a harder case built on ongoing, diffuse costs that never produced one dramatic, fundable moment.
items.reference:
Incident-driven case: concrete, dated, easy to point to. No-incident case: diffuse costs (onboarding time, search friction) accumulated across years, harder to attach a single funding trigger to.

Why: the playbook's steps don't change, but the argument for funding them does when there's no incident to point to.

items.prompt: Why might design debt with no single forcing incident actually be harder to get funded remediation for than Northwind's incident-driven case, even if the underlying debt is just as severe?
choices: Because diffuse, ongoing costs (slower onboarding, more search time, more confusion) don't compress into one dated, attributable event the way a six-hour outage does, making the case for funding an inventory less immediately compelling to leadership
Because debt without an incident is judged genuinely less severe than debt that eventually causes one, so the lower urgency is accurate rather than just a funding-optics problem
Because leadership is described as structurally unable to approve any project unless an associated incident report already exists to justify it
Because running a full component inventory is described as only being technically possible in direct response to an incident having already occurred
items.explanation: A six-hour customer-visible incident is concrete and easy to attach a cost to. Diffuse costs accumulating quietly across years are just as real but harder to point to as a single, fundable trigger — which is exactly the asymmetry the closing question asks the reader to reason through.
items.reference:
Incident-driven case: concrete, dated, easy to point to. No-incident case: diffuse costs (onboarding time, search friction) accumulated across years, harder to attach a single funding trigger to.

Why: the playbook's steps don't change, but the argument for funding them does when there's no incident to point to.
